## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")\]

[William Peter Blatty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Peter_Blatty "William Peter Blatty"), who wrote *[The Exorcist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist_\(novel\) "The Exorcist (novel)")* novel and the screenplay for [its film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist "The Exorcist"), initially had no desire to write a sequel. However, he eventually came up with a story titled *[Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_\(Blatty_novel\) "Legion (Blatty novel)")*, featuring Lieutenant William F. Kinderman, a prominent character in the original *Exorcist* novel (though he played a minor role in the eventual film), as the protagonist.[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14) Blatty conceived *Legion* as a feature film with [William Friedkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Friedkin "William Friedkin"), director of *The Exorcist*, attached to direct. Despite the critical and commercial failure of the previous sequel *[Exorcist II: The Heretic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorcist_II:_The_Heretic "Exorcist II: The Heretic")*, [Warner Bros. Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Pictures "Warner Bros. Pictures") was keen to proceed with Blatty and Friedkin's plans for another *Exorcist* film. Blatty said that "everybody wanted *Exorcist III*… I hadn't written the script, but I had the story in my head… and Billy \[Friedkin\] loved it". Friedkin, however, soon left the project due to conflicting opinions between him and Blatty on the film.[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14)

The project went into [development hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_hell "Development hell"), and Blatty wrote *Legion* as a novel instead, published in 1983\. It was a bestseller. Blatty then decided to turn the book back into a screenplay. Blatty had a meeting with Steve Jaffe who had been the publicist for both his original *Exorcist* novel and the original film. He told Jaffe of the problem he had with getting *Legion* produced because none of the studios would allow him to direct the film. Jaffe agreed to try and package it for Blatty and secured a deal with the film company that would finally make the film. Jaffe served as associate producer on *Exorcist III*.[\[14\]](#cite_note-15)\[*[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*\] Film companies [Morgan Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Creek_Productions "Morgan Creek Productions") and [Carolco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolco_Pictures "Carolco Pictures") both wanted to make the film; Blatty decided upon Morgan Creek after [Carolco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolco_Pictures "Carolco Pictures") suggested the idea of a grown-up [Regan MacNeil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regan_MacNeil "Regan MacNeil") giving birth to possessed twins.[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14)

Blatty offered directorial responsibilities to [John Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carpenter "John Carpenter"). Carpenter was initially interested, but eventually backed out over creative differences. In the book *John Carpenter: The Prince of Darkness*, Carpenter explained his reasons for not directing the film: "I met with Blatty over the course of a week, perhaps a week and a half. He had director approval, so he was testing and probing me to find out who I was and how smart I was and whether or not I should direct \[the film\]. I was ambivalent about the script, primarily because it didn't have an exorcism. Our time together was a lot of fun. We talked about everything. I kept suggesting a third-act exorcism and pushing the both of us to come up with some new, exciting, and grotesque devil gags. Blatty was resistant. He wanted to direct it and wanted to stay very close to his novel. I respected Blatty, figured out that he really wanted badly to direct the picture, and felt that I couldn't get what I needed. So I withdrew from *The Exorcist III*."[\[15\]](#cite_note-16) As per the stipulations for his deal with Morgan Creek, Blatty was to direct the movie himself, and it was to be filmed on location in [Georgetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_\(Washington,_D.C.\) "Georgetown (Washington, D.C.)").[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14)

### Casting

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Casting")\]

The central role of Lt. Kinderman had to be recast, as [Lee J. Cobb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_J._Cobb "Lee J. Cobb"), who played the part in *The Exorcist*, had died in 1976\. [George C. Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_C._Scott "George C. Scott") signed up for the role, impressed by Blatty's screenplay: "It's a horror film and much more… It's a real drama, intricately crafted, with offbeat interesting characters… and that's what makes it genuinely frightening."[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14)

Several cast members from Blatty's previous film *[The Ninth Configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ninth_Configuration "The Ninth Configuration")* (1980) appear in *The Exorcist III*: [Jason Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Miller_\(playwright\) "Jason Miller (playwright)"), reprising the role of Father [Damien Karras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damien_Karras "Damien Karras") from *The Exorcist* (billed only as "Patient X" in the end credits); [Ed Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Flanders "Ed Flanders"), taking on the role of Father Joseph Dyer (previously played by [William O'Malley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_O'Malley_\(Jesuit\) "William O'Malley (Jesuit)")); [George DiCenzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_DiCenzo "George DiCenzo") and [Scott Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Wilson_\(actor\) "Scott Wilson (actor)"). There are also [cameo appearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameo_appearance "Cameo appearance") by basketball player [Patrick Ewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Ewing "Patrick Ewing") and his college coach [John Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Thompson_\(basketball\) "John Thompson (basketball)"), model [Fabio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabio_Lanzoni "Fabio Lanzoni"), ex-Surgeon General [C. Everett Koop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Everett_Koop "C. Everett Koop"), television host [Larry King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_King "Larry King"), and an early appearance by [Samuel L. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_L._Jackson "Samuel L. Jackson") in a dream sequence. [Zohra Lampert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zohra_Lampert "Zohra Lampert"), who plays Kinderman's wife Mary, is remembered for her lead role in another horror film, 1971's *[Let's Scare Jessica to Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's_Scare_Jessica_to_Death "Let's Scare Jessica to Death")*.

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")\]

With an $11 million budget, the tentatively-titled *Exorcist: Legion* was shot on location in Georgetown for eight weeks in mid-1989. Additional interior filming took place in DEG Studios in [Wilmington, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_North_Carolina "Wilmington, North Carolina").[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14) Blatty completed [principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") of the film on time, and only slightly over budget. However, four months later, Morgan Creek informed Blatty that a new ending had to be shot. Blatty said that "[James Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Robinson "James G. Robinson"), the owner of the company, \[had a\] secretary \[who\] had insisted to him that this has nothing to do with *The Exorcist*. There had to be an exorcism."[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14) [20th Century Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Studios "20th Century Studios") put up an additional $4 million in post production to film an effects-laden exorcism sequence featuring [Nicol Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol_Williamson "Nicol Williamson") as Father Paul Morning, a character added just for the new climax. [Brad Dourif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Dourif "Brad Dourif"), who initially portrayed the dual role of Damien Karras and James Venamun, the Gemini Killer, was re-cast with Jason Miller. When Miller proved unable to recite a lot of his scenes due to his severe alcoholism, Blatty decided to call Dourif back for the role of the latter. Dourif agreed on the condition that he would be provided a hotel room where he could have ample time to rehearse with an acting assistant, as he needed to again channel the essence he had lost in the past months after portraying the character during the first round of principal photography. All scenes with Dourif in the final cut had been entirely re-shot in [Hollywood Center Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset_Las_Palmas_Studios "Sunset Las Palmas Studios") in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), California; a performance he was not completely satisfied with, as felt he gave a much stronger interpretation when they filmed in Wilmington. Blatty had to make the best of it in the narrative while racing to complete the film.

Blatty confirmed that when the possessed Karras speaks in an asexual voice, saying, "I must save my son, the Gemini," that this is, in fact, either a returned [Pazuzu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazuzu_\(The_Exorcist\) "Pazuzu (The Exorcist)") or, as Blatty put it, "[Old Scratch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Scratch "Old Scratch") himself" taking control. This ties into the revelation earlier in the film that the Gemini was sent into Karras' body as revenge for the Regan MacNeil exorcism. The altered voice in the climax is deliberately similar to that of [Mercedes McCambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_McCambridge "Mercedes McCambridge"), who did the uncredited voice of the demon in *The Exorcist*, and the role is essayed in *The Exorcist III* by [Colleen Dewhurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleen_Dewhurst "Colleen Dewhurst"), who was uncredited (actress Dewhurst was twice married to, and twice divorced from, actor George C. Scott). One scene missing from the re-filmed climax, but which appears in the trailer, shows Karras/the Gemini Killer "morphing" through a variety of faces. It was left out of the film because Blatty was not happy with the special effects work.

On the climactic exorcism scene, Blatty later said: "It's all right, but it's utterly unnecessary and it changes the character of the piece."[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14) Although at the time, Blatty told the press that he was happy to re-shoot the film's ending and have the story climax with a frenzy of special effects, apparently this compromise was forced on Blatty against his wishes:

> The original story that I sold \[Morgan Creek\] (and that I shot) ended with Kinderman blowing away Patient X. There was no exorcism. But it was a [Mexican stand-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_standoff "Mexican standoff") between me and the studio. I was entitled to one preview, then they could go and do what they wanted with the picture. They gave me a preview but it was the lowest end preview audience I have ever seen in my life. They dragged in zombies from Haiti to watch this film. It was unbelievable. But I decided, better I should do it than anyone else. I foolishly thought: I can do a good exorcism, I'll turn this pig's ear into a silk purse. So I did it.[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14)

Working on the film, Brad Dourif recalled: "We all felt really bad about it. But Blatty tried to do his best under very difficult circumstances. And I remember George C. Scott saying that the folks would only be satisfied if [Madonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna_\(entertainer\) "Madonna (entertainer)") came out and sang a song at the end!"[\[9\]](#cite_note-NinthConf-9) Dourif feels that "the original version was a hell of a lot purer and I liked it much more. As it stands now, it's a mediocre film. There are parts that have no right to be there."[\[8\]](#cite_note-A_Legion_of_Interference-8)

The execution-style ending that Blatty pitched to the studio – which was in the shooting script and actually filmed – differs radically from the ending of both the novel and the first screenplay adaption developed from the novel.[\[16\]](#cite_note-ClassicScreenplays-17) The novel ends with the Gemini Killer summoning Kinderman to his cell for a final speech and then willingly dropping dead after his alcoholic, abusive father Karl, a Christian evangelist, dies a natural death from a heart attack. As his motive for the killing was always to shame his father, the Gemini Killer's purpose for remaining on Earth no longer exists and he kills Karras in order to leave his host body. In Blatty's original screenplay adaptation, the ending is similar to the novel except that the Gemini Killer's death is not self-induced but forced supernaturally and suddenly by Karl's sudden death. In both novel and early screenplay, the Gemini Killer's motives for his murders are also given further context via a long series of flashbacks that portray his and his brother Thomas' childhood and their relationship with Karl.

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Release")\]

*The Exorcist III* was first released in October 1989 in the European MIFED ([Mercato internazionale del film e del documentario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercato_internazionale_del_film_e_del_documentario?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mercato internazionale del film e del documentario (page does not exist)") \[[it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercato%20internazionale%20del%20film%20e%20del%20documentario "it:Mercato internazionale del film e del documentario"); [fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercato%20internazionale%20del%20film%20e%20del%20documentario "fr:Mercato internazionale del film e del documentario")\]) Film Market and then opened in 1,288 theaters in the United States on August 17, 1990\. Unlike its predecessors, it was distributed by 20th Century Fox instead of Warner Bros. (though some distribution rights would later revert to Warner). The film was released only a month before the *Exorcist* [parody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody "Parody") *[Repossessed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repossessed_\(film\) "Repossessed (film)")*, starring [Linda Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Blair "Linda Blair") and [Leslie Nielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Nielsen "Leslie Nielsen"). Blair claimed that *Exorcist III* was rush-released ahead of *Repossessed*, hijacking the latter's publicity and forcing the comedy to be released a month later than was originally intended.[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14)

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

As of April 2026[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit), review aggregate website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") reported that 60% of critics gave the film positive write-ups based on 47 reviews. The critical consensus reads: "*The Exorcist III* is a talky, literary sequel with some scary moments that rival anything from the original."[\[17\]](#cite_note-rt-18) Audiences surveyed by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film a grade "C" on scale of A to F.[\[18\]](#cite_note-19)

British film critic [Mark Kermode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kermode "Mark Kermode") called it "a restrained, haunting chiller which stimulates the adrenaline and intellect alike",[\[19\]](#cite_note-20) and *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* reviewer [Vincent Canby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Canby "Vincent Canby") said "*The Exorcist III* is a better and funnier (intentionally) movie than either of its predecessors."[\[20\]](#cite_note-21) Critic Brian McKay of efilmcritic.com remarked that the movie is "not quite as chilling as the first story" yet "is at least a quality sequel", being worth watching but suffering from many "uneven" aspects.[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-11) *[People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_\(magazine\) "People (magazine)")* writer Ralph Novak began his review with, "as a movie writer-director, William Peter Blatty is like [David Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lynch "David Lynch")'s good twin: he is eccentric, original, funny and daring, but he also has a sense of taste, pace, and restraint \- which is by way of saying that this is one of the shrewdest, wittiest, most intense and most satisfying horror movies ever made".

[Owen Gleiberman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Gleiberman "Owen Gleiberman") of *[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")* wrote: "If Part II sequels are generally disappointing, Part IIIs are often much, much worse. It can seem as if nothing is going on in them except dim murmurings about the original movie — murmurings that mostly remind you of what isn't being delivered." He additionally labeled *The Exorcist III* "an ash-gray disaster \[that\] has the feel of a nightmare catechism lesson, or a horror movie made by a depressed monk".[\[21\]](#cite_note-22) In the British magazine *[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_\(magazine\) "Empire (magazine)")*, film critic [Kim Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Newman "Kim Newman") claimed that "the major fault in *Exorcist III* is the house-of-cards plot that is constantly collapsing."[\[22\]](#cite_note-23) [Kevin Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Thomas_\(film_critic\) "Kevin Thomas (film critic)") of the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* called *The Exorcist III* "a handsome, classy art film" that "doesn't completely work but offers much more than countless, less ambitious films".[\[23\]](#cite_note-24)

### Box office

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Box office")\]

*The Exorcist III* opened in first place in its opening weekend, earning $9,312,219 in the United States and Canada. It grossed a total of $26,098,824 in the United States and Canada and $18 million internationally for a total of $44 million worldwide.[\[24\]](#cite_note-25)[\[3\]](#cite_note-ww-3) Blatty attributed its poor box office performance to the title imposed by Morgan Creek, having always intended for the film to retain the title of the novel. During development and production, the film went under various titles, including *The Exorcist: 1990*. Morgan Creek and Fox insisted on including the word *Exorcist* in the title, which producer [Carter DeHaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_DeHaven "Carter DeHaven") and Blatty protested against:

> I begged them when they were considering titles not to name it *Exorcist* anything \-- because *Exorcist II* was a disaster beyond imagination. You can't call it *Exorcist III*, because people will shun the box office. But they went and named it *Exorcist III*. Then they called me after the third week when we were beginning to fade at the box office and they said 'We'll tell you the reason: it's gonna hurt, you're not gonna like this – the reason is *Exorcist II'*. I couldn't believe it! They had total amnesia about my warnings![\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14)

### Awards and nominations

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Awards and nominations")\]

In 1991, the film won a [Saturn Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_Awards "Saturn Awards") from the [Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Science_Fiction,_Fantasy_and_Horror_Films "Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror Films"), for [Best Writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_Award_for_Best_Writing "Saturn Award for Best Writing") (William Peter Blatty) and was nominated for [Best Supporting Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Saturn Award for Best Supporting Actor") ([Brad Dourif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Dourif "Brad Dourif")) and [Best Horror Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_Award_for_Best_Horror_Film "Saturn Award for Best Horror Film") at the [17th Saturn Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Saturn_Awards "17th Saturn Awards"). George C. Scott was also nominated for a [Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Raspberry_Award_for_Worst_Actor "Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Actor") but lost to [Andrew Dice Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Dice_Clay "Andrew Dice Clay") for *[The Adventures of Ford Fairlane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventures_of_Ford_Fairlane "The Adventures of Ford Fairlane")*. at the [11th Golden Raspberry Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_Golden_Raspberry_Awards "11th Golden Raspberry Awards").[\[25\]](#cite_note-26)

## Director's cut

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Director's cut")\]

Despite his misgivings about the studio-imposed reshoots, Blatty remarked on his pride in the finished version of *Exorcist III*: "It's still a superior film. And in my opinion, and excuse me if I utter heresy here, but for me... it's a more frightening film than *The Exorcist*."[\[13\]](#cite_note-TEOTS-14) Blatty hoped to recover the deleted footage from the Morgan Creek vaults so that he might re-assemble the original cut of the film which he said was "rather different" from what was released, and a version of the film which fans of the *Exorcist* series have been clamoring for. In 2007, Blatty's wife Julie Witbrodt reported on a [fan site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fansite "Fansite") that "my husband tells me that it is Morgan Creek's claim that they have lost all the footage, including an alternative opening scene, in which Kinderman views the body of Karras in the morgue, right after his fall down the steps." However, film critic [Mark Kermode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kermode "Mark Kermode") has stated that the search for the missing footage is "ongoing".[\[26\]](#cite_note-27)

Some pictures (lobby cards, stills) show a few [deleted scenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deleted_scene "Deleted scene") from Blatty's original cut of the film:

- An alternative opening scene in which Kinderman views the body of Karras in the morgue after his fall down the stairs in the ending of the first film. When Kinderman leaves the morgue, the heart monitor shows signs of life from the body of Karras.

- The aftermath of the death scene of the first murdered priest Father Tom Kanavan ([Harry Carey Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Carey_Jr. "Harry Carey Jr.")), where his dead body is shown holding his severed head while sitting.

- A longer version of the scene where Kinderman talks with Father Riley ([Lee Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Richardson_\(actor\) "Lee Richardson (actor)")) about the murders and when a demon face is shown on the statue of the saint. Originally, an unseen intruder cuts the statue's head and places a knife in its hand.

- The exhumation of Damien Karras' body in Jesuit cemetery. Later it is discovered that dead body is actually from Brother Fain, a Jesuit who was tending Karras's body and who disappeared 15 years ago. Although this scene is deleted, parts of it are used in a new ending where Patient X/Karras is buried.

- Blatty's original cut did not have Jason Miller as Karras/Patient X in it, and it had a different isolation cell for scenes in which Kinderman talked with Patient X/Gemini killer. Some promotional photos show Patient X and Kinderman talking in the original cell.

- New exorcism ending that Blatty had to film also had a small part deleted in which Karras/Patient X is morphing through many other faces. One theatrical trailer shows this deleted scene.[\[27\]](#cite_note-28)

In March 2011, a fan edit called *Legion* appeared on the Internet, credited to a fan using the pseudonym Spicediver, which removed all exorcism elements and recreated the main story arc of the director's cut without the use of any lost footage. In 2012, cast member Dourif agreed to present a screening of the fan edit at the Mad Monster Party horror convention held in [Charlotte, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte,_North_Carolina "Charlotte, North Carolina"), on March 25\. Dourif introduced the film, and did a Q&A session with the audience afterwards.[\[28\]](#cite_note-29)

In December 2015, Morgan Creek began hinting via its [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") feed that the director's cut was discovered and would eventually be released. Blatty later wrote on his website: "\[Morgan Creek\] are planning a new [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") of 'my cut'".[\[29\]](#cite_note-30) On October 25, 2016, [Scream Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shout!_Studios "Shout! Studios") released a two-disc Collector's Edition of the film, including the supposedly lost footage.[\[30\]](#cite_note-31) The website states: "We know that the biggest question you might have is: Will there be a 'Director's Cut' of the film? The answer is yes—but with some caveats. We are working on putting together a version that will be close to Blatty's original script using a mixture of various film and videotape sources that we have been provided with."

In speaking to the process of creating the *Legion* director's cut, Blu-ray producer Cliff MacMillan explains further as to the journey to get there and the outcome: "We conducted an exhaustive search through a pallet of film assets from the original shoot to re-create William Peter Blatty's intended vision. Unfortunately, that footage has been lost to time. To that end, we turned to [VHS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VHS "VHS") tapes of the film's dailies to assemble the director's cut. However, even some of that footage was incomplete, so scenes from the theatrical re-shoot were used to fill in the gaps. This director's cut is a composite of varying footage quality from the best available sources."

## Legacy

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Exorcist_III&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Legacy")\]

The film became a focal point of the trial of serial killer [Jeffrey Dahmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Dahmer "Jeffrey Dahmer"). Detectives testified that Dahmer claimed to identify with the Gemini Killer and would play the film for some of his victims before killing them. Dahmer's final attempted victim, Tracy Edwards, testified that Dahmer would rock back and forth while chanting at various times and that he especially enjoyed a sequence with a possessed Karras. Dahmer went so far as to purchase yellow contact lenses to more resemble Miller, as well as to emulate another film character he admired, [Emperor Palpatine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palpatine "Palpatine") ([Ian McDiarmid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_McDiarmid "Ian McDiarmid")) from *[Return of the Jedi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_of_the_Jedi "Return of the Jedi")* (1983).[\[31\]](#cite_note-32)

The third film in Romero's *[Night of the Living Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead_\(film_series\) "Night of the Living Dead (film series)")* series, it stars [Lori Cardille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori_Cardille "Lori Cardille"), [Terry Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Alexander_\(actor\) "Terry Alexander (actor)"), [Joseph Pilato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Pilato "Joseph Pilato"), [Jarlath Conroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarlath_Conroy "Jarlath Conroy") and [Richard Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Liberty "Richard Liberty") as members of a group of survivors of a [zombie apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie_apocalypse "Zombie apocalypse") sheltering in an underground bunker in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), where they must determine the outcome of humanity's conflict with the undead horde. Romero described the film as a "tragedy about how a lack of human communication causes chaos and collapse even in this small little pie slice of society".[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) Line 273: Work on *Day of the Dead* began shortly after the release of the previous film in the series, *[Dawn of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_of_the_Dead_\(1978_film\) "Dawn of the Dead (1978 film)")* (1978), but was halted when Romero began work on other projects. It was developed as part of a three-film deal with that film's distributor, United Film Distribution Company (UFDC); Romero elected to make the two other projects outlined in the deal, *[Knightriders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knightriders "Knightriders")* (1981) and *[Creepshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creepshow "Creepshow")* (1982), first. Although the filmmaker was given [final cut privilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_cut_privilege "Final cut privilege"), the screenplay was rewritten multiple times due to UFDC's concerns that Romero's ambitious original vision ― which he described as "the *[Gone with the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gone_with_the_Wind_\(film\) "Gone with the Wind (film)")* of zombie films" ― would need to be shot with the intention of receiving an [R rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association_film_rating_system "Motion Picture Association film rating system") from the [Motion Picture Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association "Motion Picture Association") to ensure its commercial viability; Romero elected to make the film on a lower budget and release it without a rating. *Day of the Dead* was filmed in fall 1984, with above-ground scenes in the cities of [Fort Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Myers,_Florida "Fort Myers, Florida") and [Sanibel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanibel,_Florida "Sanibel, Florida") and underground scenes near [Wampum, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wampum,_Pennsylvania "Wampum, Pennsylvania"). [Tom Savini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Savini "Tom Savini") returned to provide the film's [special make-up effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wi... Line 275: *Day of the Dead* premiered in [Hicksville, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hicksville,_New_York "Hicksville, New York") on June 30, 1985, and grossed $34 million worldwide against a budget of approximately $4 million. Although the make-up effects were praised, the film initially did not match the critical and commercial success of its predecessors; the series did not see another installment until the 2005 release of *[Land of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_of_the_Dead "Land of the Dead")*. Reception of the film has improved with time, and Romero deemed it to be his personal favorite film in the original *Dead* trilogy. Like its predecessors, *Day of the Dead* has garnered a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_film "Cult film") and inspired numerous parodies and homages. Line 277: The film was remade twice: the first is the [2008 film of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead_\(2008_film\) "Day of the Dead (2008 film)"), and the second is *[Day of the Dead: Bloodline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead:_Bloodline "Day of the Dead: Bloodline")* (2017). A [television series named after the film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead_\(TV_series\) "Day of the Dead (TV series)") began airing on [Syfy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syfy "Syfy") in 2021, while a [stand-alone sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-alone_sequel "Stand-alone sequel"), *Night of the Living Dead II*, was reported to be in active development.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Line 349: The film was given a very limited release.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FI-8) This is chronicled in the documentary *The Many Days of 'Day of the Dead'* on the two-disc [Anchor Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchor_Bay_Entertainment "Anchor Bay Entertainment") special edition DVD of the film.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FI-8) Some of the original concepts and characters remain, but the film differs greatly from Romero's original script,[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) as stated by actress [Lori Cardille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori_Cardille "Lori Cardille"): Line 359: The role of Dr. Matthew "Frankenstein" Logan was played by [Richard Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Liberty "Richard Liberty"). Line 383: *Day of the Dead* would peak at 23 on the *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* chart *Top VHS Sales* in 1986 a year after its initial release.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) Line 385: The film grossed $5.8 million domestically.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FI-8) It fared much better internationally, grossing $28.2 million outside of the United States.[\[14\]](#cite_note-DAYBOXW-14) *Day of the Dead*'s total gross is a little over $34 million.[\[14\]](#cite_note-DAYBOXW-14) The film is also noted for its [special effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_effect "Special effect") work, notably [Tom Savini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Savini "Tom Savini")'s make-up, he was honored with his second [Saturn Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_Awards "Saturn Awards") in 1985 for Best Make-up, the first time being with *Dawn of the Dead* in 1980\.[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) [Jonathan Rosenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Rosenbaum "Jonathan Rosenbaum") placed the film in his personal canon of 1,000 favorite films, one of two Romero films chosen by Rosenbaum (the other was *[Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_\(1977_film\) "Martin (1977 film)")*).[\[32\]](#cite_note-32) Romero himself cited *Day of the Dead* as his personal favorite of his original trilogy of zombie films.[\[33\]](#cite_note-33) On May 19, 2012, the film headlined the 12-hour film festival Hudson Horror Show V.[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) Line 387: [Alex Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Stewart_\(writer\) "Alex Stewart (writer)") reviewed *Day of the Dead* for *[White Dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Dwarf_\(magazine\) "White Dwarf (magazine)")* \#83, and stated that "Organized around a tough performance by Lori Cardille as the determined research leader, the movie is as much a study of the several inhumanities of science and the military as it is a feast of gore and putrefaction. After all, disembowelling is only one way, the most literal, of taking people apart."[\[35\]](#cite_note-35) Line 393: The film was released on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") on November 24, 1998 in the United States and on March 5, 2001 in the United Kingdom.[\[25\]](#cite_note-Haflidason-25)[\[36\]](#cite_note-36) Both the theatrical and an unrated [director's cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director's_cut "Director's cut") were released as special editions containing identical bonus features, and the DVD was released in the United Kingdom in a region 2 DVD.[\[25\]](#cite_note-Haflidason-25) The [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") version of *Day of the Dead* was released on October 2, 2007\.[\[37\]](#cite_note-Blu-ray-37) This edition includes many special features, including two audio commentary tracks with writer-director [George A. Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_A._Romero "George A. Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_A._Romero "George A. Romero"), and produced by [Richard P. Rubinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_P._Rubinstein "Richard P. Rubinstein"). The third film in Romero's *[Night of the Living Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead_\(film_series\) "Night of the Living Dead (film series)")* series, it stars [Lori Cardille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori_Cardille "Lori Cardille"), [Terry Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Alexander_\(actor\) "Terry Alexander (actor)"), [Joseph Pilato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Pilato "Joseph Pilato"), [Jarlath Conroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarlath_Conroy "Jarlath Conroy") and [Richard Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Liberty "Richard Liberty") as members of a group of survivors of a [zombie apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie_apocalypse "Zombie apocalypse") sheltering in an underground bunker in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), where they must determine the outcome of humanity's conflict with the undead horde. Romero described the film as a "tragedy about how a lack of human communication causes chaos and collapse even in this small little pie slice of society".[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) Line 273: Work on *Day of the Dead* began shortly after the release of the previous film in the series, *[Dawn of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_of_the_Dead_\(1978_film\) "Dawn of the Dead (1978 film)")* (1978), but was halted when Romero began work on other projects. It was developed as part of a three-film deal with that film's distributor, United Film Distribution Company (UFDC); Romero elected to make the two other projects outlined in the deal, *[Knightriders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knightriders "Knightriders")* (1981) and *[Creepshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creepshow "Creepshow")* (1982), first. Although the filmmaker was given [final cut privilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_cut_privilege "Final cut privilege"), the screenplay was rewritten multiple times due to UFDC's concerns that Romero's ambitious original vision ― which he described as "the *[Gone with the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gone_with_the_Wind_\(film\) "Gone with the Wind (film)")* of zombie films" ― would need to be shot with the intention of receiving an [R rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association_film_rating_system "Motion Picture Association film rating system") from the [Motion Picture Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association "Motion Picture Association") to ensure its commercial viability; Romero elected to make the film on a lower budget and release it without a rating. *Day of the Dead* was filmed in fall 1984, with above-ground scenes in the cities of [Fort Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Myers,_Florida "Fort Myers, Florida") and [Sanibel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanibel,_Florida "Sanibel, Florida") and underground scenes near [Wampum, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wampum,_Pennsylvania "Wampum, Pennsylvania"). [Tom Savini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Savini "Tom Savini") returned to provide the film's [special make-up effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wi... Line 275: *Day of the Dead* premiered in [Hicksville, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hicksville,_New_York "Hicksville, New York") on June 30, 1985, and grossed $34 million worldwide against a budget of approximately $4 million. Although the make-up effects were praised, the film initially did not match the critical and commercial success of its predecessors; the series did not see another installment until the 2005 release of *[Land of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_of_the_Dead "Land of the Dead")*. Reception of the film has improved with time, and Romero deemed it to be his personal favorite film in the original *Dead* trilogy. Like its predecessors, *Day of the Dead* has garnered a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_film "Cult film") and inspired numerous parodies and homages. Line 277: The film was remade twice: the first is the [2008 film of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead_\(2008_film\) "Day of the Dead (2008 film)"), and the second is *[Day of the Dead: Bloodline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead:_Bloodline "Day of the Dead: Bloodline")* (2017). Wish Upon

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/67/Wish_upon_ver2.jpg/250px-Wish_upon_ver2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wish_upon_ver2.jpg) Theatrical release poster

***Wish Upon*** is a 2017 American [supernatural horror film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_horror_film "Supernatural horror film"), directed by [John R. Leonetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Leonetti "John R. Leonetti"), written by Barbara Marshall, and starring [Joey King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_King "Joey King"), [Ki Hong Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ki_Hong_Lee "Ki Hong Lee"), [Sydney Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Park_\(actress\) "Sydney Park (actress)"), [Shannon Purser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Purser "Shannon Purser"), [Sherilyn Fenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherilyn_Fenn "Sherilyn Fenn"), [Elisabeth Rohm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Rohm "Elisabeth Rohm"), and [Ryan Phillippe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Phillippe "Ryan Phillippe"). The film follows a teenage girl who is given a magic music box that grants seven wishes, but kills someone close to her each time it does.

The film was theatrically released on July 14, 2017, by [Broad Green Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Green_Pictures "Broad Green Pictures") and [Orion Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_Pictures "Orion Pictures"). It received negative reviews from critics and grossed $23.5 million worldwide against a $12 million budget.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

Clare Shannon, a seventeen-year-old high school outcast, is haunted by the memory of her mother's suicide that she witnessed as a young child.

Her father, Jonathan, a hoarder and dumpster diver, finds a Chinese music box and gives it to Clare. She deciphers one of the inscriptions on the box as "Seven Wishes", and absentmindedly wishes for Darcie, her school bully, to "rot", at which point Darcie develops [necrotizing fasciitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necrotizing_fasciitis "Necrotizing fasciitis"). That same day, Clare's dog Max dies. Clare deduces the box grants wishes.

Clare makes a second wish that a popular boy named Paul would fall madly in love with her and he does (so much he starts to stalk her). That same night, her wealthy great-uncle dies. Hearing this, Clare wishes to be in his will, which leaves everything to her. Consequently, their neighbor Mrs. Deluca dies.

Clare enlists the help of classmate Ryan Hui to translate the symbols on the box. His cousin Gina is able to decipher that each of the seven wishes comes with consequences and the box belonged to a Chinese woman named Lu Mei. During a 1910 outbreak of [bubonic plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubonic_plague "Bubonic plague") in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), Mei's family was forcibly quarantined in a railroad car where all but Mei died of starvation. Mei prayed for revenge and offered up her family's only valuable heirloom, the music box, as a sacrifice. A demonic Yaoguai spirit answered her prayer, cursing the box. After using the box to get her revenge, Mei committed suicide.

Clare makes a fourth wish that her father will stop being so embarrassing; he stops dumpster diving and starts playing the saxophone again. Gina learns the meaning of the final phrase on the box: "When the music ends, the blood price is paid." Before she can warn Ryan, she is impaled on a statue in her loft and dies. After Ryan finds Gina's body, he angrily confronts Clare.

Despite now knowing about the "blood price", Clare is in denial and makes a fifth wish to be the most popular girl in school. She is soon unhappy with the loss of her relationship with her best friends, Meredith and June, and her constant nightmares. She breaks up with Paul after discovering he has been stalking her and sneaking into her house at night. Meredith dies when the elevator she is in plummets 30 floors.

Ryan reveals that after the seventh wish, the Yaoguai will claim the soul of the box's owner and all previous owners died tragically. The box cannot be destroyed so Clare hides it in an air vent. Paul breaks into her house and threatens her, unable to accept the end of their relationship. He attempts suicide and is taken away in an ambulance. June steals the box, knowing Clare will not get rid of it. Per the rules of the box, Clare loses everything she'd wished for and returns to her previous existence, miserable. Addicted to the power, she wrestles the box back from June, frustrating Ryan, who blames her for the string of deaths. Her sixth wish is that her mother never committed suicide and her reality changes, with her mother now alive and two younger sisters who did not previously exist.

While rummaging through her mother's paintings, Clare finds a painting of the music box, discovering that her mother was a previous owner, which led to her suicide. She hysterically runs to protect her father but is too late; her father is decapitated by a running chainsaw. Frantic, Clare makes her seventh wish – to go back to the morning her father found the box.

That morning, Clare finds the box moments before her father, preventing the tragic sequence of events. At school, she asks Ryan to bury the box for her and kisses him. However, she is immediately killed when she's hit by Darcie's car, the Yaoguai having claimed her soul just like her mother.

In a mid-credits scene, Ryan prepares to bury the music box, but becomes intrigued by the inscription about the seven wishes.

## Themes

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")\]

Director John R. Leonetti summarized *Wish Upon* as different from similar "[The Monkey's Paw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Monkey's_Paw "The Monkey's Paw")"-esque stories for the depth of the character Clare, particularly her tough childhood and the inability to stop using the music box even as she realizes what it really does.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")\]

The film is loosely based on [W. W. Jacobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._W._Jacobs "W. W. Jacobs")' short story *[The Monkey's Paw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Monkey's_Paw "The Monkey's Paw")*. The film's screenplay was voted to the 2015 [Black List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_List_\(survey\) "Black List (survey)").[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) [Catherine Hardwicke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Hardwicke "Catherine Hardwicke") was originally planned to direct the film, but she later was removed from the project. Afterward, producer Sherryl Clark sent a draft of the script to [John R. Leonetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Leonetti "John R. Leonetti"); he explained that while he did enjoy the script, "I didn't completely jump on at first because I had other things going on."[\[5\]](#cite_note-Weintraub-2017-5) However, another draft sent by Clark four months later caught his eye, and he took on directing duties from there.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Weintraub-2017-5) While most of the contents of the original drafts were seen in the final cut, there were alterations. A sequence where Carl almost gets hit by a truck, which referenced Billy Hitchcock's death in *[Final Destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination_\(film\) "Final Destination (film)")* (2000), was removed as the filmmakers ultimately didn't want to make a *Final Destination*\-esque product.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Weintraub-2017-5) During filming, the scene of Jonathan in his car with a flat tire was pulled "right out of our ass" to serve as a diversion to Meredith's elevator death.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Weintraub-2017-5)

On July 27, 2016, it was announced that *Wish Upon* would be directed by [John R. Leonetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Leonetti "John R. Leonetti").[\[6\]](#cite_note-Annabelle-2016-6) The film is produced by Sherryl Clark from her production company, Busted Shark Productions,[\[7\]](#cite_note-Anita_Busch-2016-7) and written by Barbara Marshall.[\[6\]](#cite_note-Annabelle-2016-6) In August 2016, [Joey King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_King "Joey King") was cast in the film's lead role,[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) and on November 9, 2016, [Ki Hong Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ki_Hong_Lee "Ki Hong Lee") was announced to have also joined.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Anita_Busch-2016-7) King was Leonetti's first choice for Clare Shannon, as the two previously worked together on *[The Conjuring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Conjuring "The Conjuring")* (2013); and the director wanted to feature [Shannon Purser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Purser "Shannon Purser") in the film after seeing her in *[Stranger Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stranger_Things "Stranger Things")*.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) The film began production in November 2016 in Toronto.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) Shot on an [Arri Alexa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arri_Alexa "Arri Alexa") at 3\.4K resolution, *Wish Upon* was directed by Leonetti to look natural, departing from the stylized visual aesthetics of other horror films.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Release")\]

### Theatrical

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Theatrical")\]

The film's teaser trailer was released on February 9, 2017\.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) The first trailer debuted on March 22, 2017,[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) and the second trailer was released on May 22, 2017\.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) *Wish Upon* was released in theaters on July 14, 2017, in the U.S., and July 28, 2017, in the U.K.[\[15\]](#cite_note-Lee-2017-15)

### Home video

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Home video")\]

*Wish Upon* was released on DVD and Blu-ray in the United States on October 10, 2017\. The Blu-ray also includes the director's Unrated Cut of the movie which is one minute longer and favoured by the director.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

### Marketing

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Marketing")\]

Broad Green Pictures granted seven fan wishes submitted via the film's official website.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Reception")\]

### Box office

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Box office")\]

*Wish Upon* grossed $14.3 million in the United States and Canada, and $9.2 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $23.5 million, against a production budget of $12 million.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

In North America, *Wish Upon* was released alongside the opening of *[War for the Planet of the Apes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_for_the_Planet_of_the_Apes "War for the Planet of the Apes")*, as well as the wide expansion of *[The Big Sick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Big_Sick "The Big Sick")*, and was projected to gross $8–10 million from 2,100 theaters in its opening weekend.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) It made $376,000 from Thursday night previews at 1,659 theaters and $2.3 million on its first day. It went on to debut to $5.5 million for its opening weekend, finishing seventh at the box office.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 20% of 91 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 4\.0/10. The website's consensus reads: "*Wish Upon* is neither scary nor original, but its fundamental flaws as a horror movie may make it destination viewing for [after-midnight camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_movie "Midnight movie") genre enthusiasts."[\[22\]](#cite_note-Rotten_Tomatoes-22) [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 32 out of 100, based on 24 critics, indicating "generally unfavorable" reviews.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Metacritic-23) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "C" on an A+ to F scale.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)

*[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Observer "The Observer")*'s Simran Hans gave the film 2/5 stars, writing, "Fashioning itself as a teen horror, *Wish Upon* is far too tame for most actual adolescents".[\[25\]](#cite_note-25) [Robbie Collin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbie_Collin "Robbie Collin") of *[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")* wrote, "*Wish Upon* tries to put a millennial spin on the premise, but fumbles everything it sets out to do so extravagantly, the film itself feels like the result of some kind of diabolical, chimpanzee-fingered pact." He gave it 1/5 stars.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) *[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times "The Times")'*s Ed Potton also gave it 1/5 stars, writing, "Seldom has a teen protagonist been as annoying as the one in this high-concept high-school horror... Somewhere in here there's a message about the perils of [peer pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_pressure "Peer pressure") and the cruelty of social media, but it's submerged below all the stagey angst and telegraphed peril. By the end you're hoping that Clare gets her just deserts."[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")*'s Benjamin Lee also gave the film 1/5 stars and wrote, "the makers have decided to scrap any vague attempt at originality and lazily smash together two other tried and tested conceits: the double-edged wishes from [*Wishmaster*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wishmaster_\(film\) "Wishmaster (film)") and the supernatural accident deaths from *[Final Destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination "Final Destination")*. What's most remarkable about the film is how it's somehow even worse than that sounds."[\[15\]](#cite_note-Lee-2017-15)

Andrew Barker of *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")* wrote, "By any normal standards, teen horror flick *Wish Upon* is a pretty bad movie. But its badness is of such a distinct and kooky character that it can't help but exert an inadvertent charm."[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) Emily Yoshida of [*Vulture*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulture_\(website\) "Vulture (website)") called the film "a deeply silly midsummer lark that makes up for the fact that it's about nothing by being incredibly entertaining."[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) The *[San Francisco Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Chronicle "San Francisco Chronicle")'*s Peter Hartlaub called it "a summer movie that delivers a lowest-common-denominator good time, and mostly succeeds", and gave it 2/4 stars.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) Katie Walsh of the [Tribune News Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribune_News_Service "Tribune News Service") called the film "a spooky teen story that's not particularly heavy on the scares, though its unintentional giggles almost ensure it a spot as a [cult movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_movie "Cult movie")."[\[31\]](#cite_note-31)

In 2023, [Red Letter Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Letter_Media "Red Letter Media") featured the film in a spotlight episode of their series *Best of the Worst*, highlighting it as a modern masterpiece of "[so bad it's good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_bad_it's_good "So bad it's good")" cinema.[\[32\]](#cite_note-32)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

2017 American horror film

Wish Upon

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/67/Wish_upon_ver2.jpg/250px-Wish_upon_ver2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wish_upon_ver2.jpg) Theatrical release poster

Directed by | [John R. Leonetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Leonetti "John R. Leonetti")

Written by | Barbara Marshall

Produced by | [Sherryl Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherryl_Clark "Sherryl Clark")

Starring | - [Joey King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_King "Joey King") - [Ki Hong Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ki_Hong_Lee "Ki Hong Lee") - [Sydney Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Park_\(actress\) "Sydney Park (actress)") - [Elisabeth Rohm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Rohm "Elisabeth Rohm") - [Ryan Phillippe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Phillippe "Ryan Phillippe")

Cinematography | Michael Galbraith

Edited by | Peck Prior

Music by | [Tomandandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomandandy "Tomandandy")

Production company | Busted Shark Productions

Distributed by | - [Broad Green Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Green_Pictures "Broad Green Pictures") - [Orion Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_Pictures "Orion Pictures")

Release date | - July 14, 2017 (2017-07-14)

Running time | 90 minutes (theatrical)[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) 91 minutes (unrated)[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)

Country | United States

Language | English

Budget | $12 million

Box office | $23.5 million

***Wish Upon*** is a 2017 American [supernatural horror film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_horror_film "Supernatural horror film"), directed by [John R. Leonetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Leonetti "John R. Leonetti"), written by Barbara Marshall, and starring [Joey King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_King "Joey King"), [Ki Hong Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ki_Hong_Lee "Ki Hong Lee"), [Sydney Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Park_\(actress\) "Sydney Park (actress)"), [Shannon Purser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Purser "Shannon Purser"), [Sherilyn Fenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherilyn_Fenn "Sherilyn Fenn"), [Elisabeth Rohm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Rohm "Elisabeth Rohm"), and [Ryan Phillippe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Phillippe "Ryan Phillippe"). The film follows a teenage girl who is given a magic music box that grants seven wishes, but kills someone close to her each time it does.

The film was theatrically released on July 14, 2017, by [Broad Green Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Green_Pictures "Broad Green Pictures") and [Orion Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_Pictures "Orion Pictures"). It received negative reviews from critics and grossed $23.5 million worldwide against a $12 million budget.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

Clare Shannon, a seventeen-year-old high school outcast, is haunted by the memory of her mother's suicide that she witnessed as a young child.

Her father, Jonathan, a hoarder and dumpster diver, finds a Chinese music box and gives it to Clare. She deciphers one of the inscriptions on the box as "Seven Wishes", and absentmindedly wishes for Darcie, her school bully, to "rot", at which point Darcie develops [necrotizing fasciitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necrotizing_fasciitis "Necrotizing fasciitis"). That same day, Clare's dog Max dies. Clare deduces the box grants wishes.

Clare makes a second wish that a popular boy named Paul would fall madly in love with her and he does (so much he starts to stalk her). That same night, her wealthy great-uncle dies. Hearing this, Clare wishes to be in his will, which leaves everything to her. Consequently, their neighbor Mrs. Deluca dies.

Clare enlists the help of classmate Ryan Hui to translate the symbols on the box. His cousin Gina is able to decipher that each of the seven wishes comes with consequences and the box belonged to a Chinese woman named Lu Mei. During a 1910 outbreak of [bubonic plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubonic_plague "Bubonic plague") in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), Mei's family was forcibly quarantined in a railroad car where all but Mei died of starvation. Mei prayed for revenge and offered up her family's only valuable heirloom, the music box, as a sacrifice. A demonic Yaoguai spirit answered her prayer, cursing the box. After using the box to get her revenge, Mei committed suicide.

Clare makes a fourth wish that her father will stop being so embarrassing; he stops dumpster diving and starts playing the saxophone again. Gina learns the meaning of the final phrase on the box: "When the music ends, the blood price is paid." Before she can warn Ryan, she is impaled on a statue in her loft and dies. After Ryan finds Gina's body, he angrily confronts Clare.

Despite now knowing about the "blood price", Clare is in denial and makes a fifth wish to be the most popular girl in school. She is soon unhappy with the loss of her relationship with her best friends, Meredith and June, and her constant nightmares. She breaks up with Paul after discovering he has been stalking her and sneaking into her house at night. Meredith dies when the elevator she is in plummets 30 floors.

Ryan reveals that after the seventh wish, the Yaoguai will claim the soul of the box's owner and all previous owners died tragically. The box cannot be destroyed so Clare hides it in an air vent. Paul breaks into her house and threatens her, unable to accept the end of their relationship. He attempts suicide and is taken away in an ambulance. June steals the box, knowing Clare will not get rid of it. Per the rules of the box, Clare loses everything she'd wished for and returns to her previous existence, miserable. Addicted to the power, she wrestles the box back from June, frustrating Ryan, who blames her for the string of deaths. Her sixth wish is that her mother never committed suicide and her reality changes, with her mother now alive and two younger sisters who did not previously exist.

While rummaging through her mother's paintings, Clare finds a painting of the music box, discovering that her mother was a previous owner, which led to her suicide. She hysterically runs to protect her father but is too late; her father is decapitated by a running chainsaw. Frantic, Clare makes her seventh wish – to go back to the morning her father found the box.

That morning, Clare finds the box moments before her father, preventing the tragic sequence of events. At school, she asks Ryan to bury the box for her and kisses him. However, she is immediately killed when she's hit by Darcie's car, the Yaoguai having claimed her soul just like her mother.

In a mid-credits scene, Ryan prepares to bury the music box, but becomes intrigued by the inscription about the seven wishes.

## Cast

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Cast")\]

## Themes

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")\]

Director John R. Leonetti summarized *Wish Upon* as different from similar "[The Monkey's Paw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Monkey's_Paw "The Monkey's Paw")"-esque stories for the depth of the character Clare, particularly her tough childhood and the inability to stop using the music box even as she realizes what it really does.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")\]

The film is loosely based on [W. W. Jacobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._W._Jacobs "W. W. Jacobs")' short story *[The Monkey's Paw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Monkey's_Paw "The Monkey's Paw")*. The film's screenplay was voted to the 2015 [Black List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_List_\(survey\) "Black List (survey)").[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) [Catherine Hardwicke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Hardwicke "Catherine Hardwicke") was originally planned to direct the film, but she later was removed from the project. Afterward, producer Sherryl Clark sent a draft of the script to [John R. Leonetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Leonetti "John R. Leonetti"); he explained that while he did enjoy the script, "I didn't completely jump on at first because I had other things going on."[\[5\]](#cite_note-Weintraub-2017-5) However, another draft sent by Clark four months later caught his eye, and he took on directing duties from there.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Weintraub-2017-5) While most of the contents of the original drafts were seen in the final cut, there were alterations. A sequence where Carl almost gets hit by a truck, which referenced Billy Hitchcock's death in *[Final Destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination_\(film\) "Final Destination (film)")* (2000), was removed as the filmmakers ultimately didn't want to make a *Final Destination*\-esque product.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Weintraub-2017-5) During filming, the scene of Jonathan in his car with a flat tire was pulled "right out of our ass" to serve as a diversion to Meredith's elevator death.[\[5\]](#cite_note-Weintraub-2017-5)

On July 27, 2016, it was announced that *Wish Upon* would be directed by [John R. Leonetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Leonetti "John R. Leonetti").[\[6\]](#cite_note-Annabelle-2016-6) The film is produced by Sherryl Clark from her production company, Busted Shark Productions,[\[7\]](#cite_note-Anita_Busch-2016-7) and written by Barbara Marshall.[\[6\]](#cite_note-Annabelle-2016-6) In August 2016, [Joey King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_King "Joey King") was cast in the film's lead role,[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) and on November 9, 2016, [Ki Hong Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ki_Hong_Lee "Ki Hong Lee") was announced to have also joined.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Anita_Busch-2016-7) King was Leonetti's first choice for Clare Shannon, as the two previously worked together on *[The Conjuring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Conjuring "The Conjuring")* (2013); and the director wanted to feature [Shannon Purser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Purser "Shannon Purser") in the film after seeing her in *[Stranger Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stranger_Things "Stranger Things")*.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) The film began production in November 2016 in Toronto.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) Shot on an [Arri Alexa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arri_Alexa "Arri Alexa") at 3\.4K resolution, *Wish Upon* was directed by Leonetti to look natural, departing from the stylized visual aesthetics of other horror films.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Release")\]

### Theatrical

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Theatrical")\]

The film's teaser trailer was released on February 9, 2017\.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) The first trailer debuted on March 22, 2017,[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) and the second trailer was released on May 22, 2017\.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) *Wish Upon* was released in theaters on July 14, 2017, in the U.S., and July 28, 2017, in the U.K.[\[15\]](#cite_note-Lee-2017-15)

### Home video

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Home video")\]

*Wish Upon* was released on DVD and Blu-ray in the United States on October 10, 2017\. The Blu-ray also includes the director's Unrated Cut of the movie which is one minute longer and favoured by the director.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

### Marketing

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Marketing")\]

Broad Green Pictures granted seven fan wishes submitted via the film's official website.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Reception")\]

### Box office

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Box office")\]

*Wish Upon* grossed $14.3 million in the United States and Canada, and $9.2 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $23.5 million, against a production budget of $12 million.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

In North America, *Wish Upon* was released alongside the opening of *[War for the Planet of the Apes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_for_the_Planet_of_the_Apes "War for the Planet of the Apes")*, as well as the wide expansion of *[The Big Sick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Big_Sick "The Big Sick")*, and was projected to gross $8–10 million from 2,100 theaters in its opening weekend.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) It made $376,000 from Thursday night previews at 1,659 theaters and $2.3 million on its first day. It went on to debut to $5.5 million for its opening weekend, finishing seventh at the box office.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wish_Upon&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 20% of 91 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 4\.0/10. The website's consensus reads: "*Wish Upon* is neither scary nor original, but its fundamental flaws as a horror movie may make it destination viewing for [after-midnight camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_movie "Midnight movie") genre enthusiasts."[\[22\]](#cite_note-Rotten_Tomatoes-22) [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 32 out of 100, based on 24 critics, indicating "generally unfavorable" reviews.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Metacritic-23) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "C" on an A+ to F scale.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)

*[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Observer "The Observer")*'s Simran Hans gave the film 2/5 stars, writing, "Fashioning itself as a teen horror, *Wish Upon* is far too tame for most actual adolescents".[\[25\]](#cite_note-25) [Robbie Collin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbie_Collin "Robbie Collin") of *[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")* wrote, "*Wish Upon* tries to put a millennial spin on the premise, but fumbles everything it sets out to do so extravagantly, the film itself feels like the result of some kind of diabolical, chimpanzee-fingered pact." He gave it 1/5 stars.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) *[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times "The Times")'*s Ed Potton also gave it 1/5 stars, writing, "Seldom has a teen protagonist been as annoying as the one in this high-concept high-school horror... Somewhere in here there's a message about the perils of [peer pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_pressure "Peer pressure") and the cruelty of social media, but it's submerged below all the stagey angst and telegraphed peril. By the end you're hoping that Clare gets her just deserts."[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")*'s Benjamin Lee also gave the film 1/5 stars and wrote, "the makers have decided to scrap any vague attempt at originality and lazily smash together two other tried and tested conceits: the double-edged wishes from [*Wishmaster*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wishmaster_\(film\) "Wishmaster (film)") and the supernatural accident deaths from *[Final Destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination "Final Destination")*. What's most remarkable about the film is how it's somehow even worse than that sounds."[\[15\]](#cite_note-Lee-2017-15)

Andrew Barker of *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")* wrote, "By any normal standards, teen horror flick *Wish Upon* is a pretty bad movie. But its badness is of such a distinct and kooky character that it can't help but exert an inadvertent charm."[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) Emily Yoshida of [*Vulture*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulture_\(website\) "Vulture (website)") called the film "a deeply silly midsummer lark that makes up for the fact that it's about nothing by being incredibly entertaining."[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) The *[San Francisco Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Chronicle "San Francisco Chronicle")'*s Peter Hartlaub called it "a summer movie that delivers a lowest-common-denominator good time, and mostly succeeds", and gave it 2/4 stars.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) Katie Walsh of the [Tribune News Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribune_News_Service "Tribune News Service") called the film "a spooky teen story that's not particularly heavy on the scares, though its unintentional giggles almost ensure it a spot as a [cult movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_movie "Cult movie")."[\[31\]](#cite_note-31)

In 2023, [Red Letter Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Letter_Media "Red Letter Media") featured the film in a spotlight episode of their series *Best of the Worst*, highlighting it as a modern masterpiece of "[so bad it's good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_bad_it's_good "So bad it's good")" cinema.[\[32\]](#cite_note-32)

#### Description by Wikipedia

Boogeyman is a 2005 supernatural horror film directed by Stephen Kay and starring Barry Watson, Emily Deschanel, Skye McCole Bartusiak, Tory Mussett, Charles Mesure, and Lucy Lawless. Written by Eric Kripke, Juliet Snowden, and Stiles White, from a story by Kripke, the film is a new take on the classic "boogeyman", or monster in the closet, who is the eponymous antagonist of the film. The plot concerns a young man returns to the house he grew up in to confront the childhood terror that has affected his life. It’s an international co-production between the United States, New Zealand and Germany.

#### Description by Wikipedia

Boogeyman is a 2005 supernatural horror film directed by Stephen Kay and starring Barry Watson, Emily Deschanel, Skye McCole Bartusiak, Tory Mussett, Charles Mesure, and Lucy Lawless. Written by Eric Kripke, Juliet Snowden, and Stiles White, from a story by Kripke, the film is a new take on the classic "boogeyman", or monster in the closet, who is the eponymous antagonist of the film. The plot concerns a young man returns to the house he grew up in to confront the childhood terror that has affected his life. It’s an international co-production between the United States, New Zealand and Germany.

import re
def parse(fn):
    cues=[]
    txt=open(fn, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()
    blocks=re.split(r'\n\s*\n', txt)
    for b in blocks:
        lines=b.strip().split('\n')
        if len(lines)>=2:
            m=re.match(r'(\d+):(\d+):(\d+)[,.](\d+)\s*-->\s*(\d+):(\d+):(\d+)', lines[1] if '-->' in lines[1] else lines[0])
            if not m and len(lines)>=3: m=re.match(r'(\d+):(\d+):(\d+)[,.](\d+)\s*-->\s*(\d+):(\d+):(\d+)', lines[1])
            if m:
                h1,mn1,s1=int(m.group(1)),int(m.group(2)),int(m.group(3))
                t=h1*3600+mn1*60+s1
                dlg=' '.join(l for l in lines if '-->' not in l and not l.strip().isdigit())
                cues.append((t,dlg))
    return cues

## How I identified it

I analyzed `barcode.png` (1000 solid-color columns; ≈5.4 s of film per column ⇒ ≈89 min, matching a 89-minute film), then located exact scene times via a subtitle file (text only, no video) and checked the barcode's color at each time:

Every distinctive feature — the early white flash, the isolated warm stripes, the two long pitch-dark stretches, the overcast middle act, and the long black ending — lands exactly on a timestamped scene.
